lesson.title: Sharing a Crowded World: The Struggle of Competition
lesson.summary: Competition happens when two or more organisms need the same limited resource, and it is one of the most powerful forces shaping where species live and how large their populations can grow.
lesson.body:
You have already seen that species interact in many ways, some helpful, some harmful, some neutral. Competition is the interaction where two or more organisms are harmed, or at least held back, because they both want the same limited thing. That thing might be food, water, sunlight, nesting sites, mates, or physical space. Resources in nature are almost never unlimited, so whenever two organisms need the same one, competition becomes possible.

Ecologists distinguish between two broad ways competition plays out. In exploitation competition, individuals do not interact directly at all. They simply use up a shared resource, so that less is left for others. Two species of seed eating birds might never fight or even see each other, but if one depletes the seed supply, the other still suffers. In interference competition, organisms interact directly, through aggression, chemical warfare, or territorial defense. A male songbird chasing a rival off its territory, or a fungus releasing chemicals that stop other fungi from growing nearby, are both examples of interference.

It also matters whether competition happens within a species (intraspecific competition) or between different species (interspecific competition). Members of the same species usually need almost identical resources, so intraspecific competition tends to be especially intense, and it is a major reason population growth slows down as a population gets crowded. This chapter focuses mainly on interspecific competition, the tension between different species, because of how strongly it shapes entire communities.

One of the clearest demonstrations of interspecific competition comes from a classic set of field experiments the ecologist Joseph Connell ran on a rocky shore in Scotland in the late 1950s and published in 1961. Two barnacle species, Chthamalus stellatus and Semibalanus balanoides, occupied overlapping zones on the shoreline rocks, but Chthamalus was mostly restricted to the higher, drier zone. Connell found that Chthamalus larvae could actually settle and survive lower down on the shore when Semibalanus was experimentally removed. Left alone, the faster growing Semibalanus crowded out and literally smothered or pried loose the Chthamalus individuals that tried to settle in the lower zone. The lower boundary of Chthamalus's distribution, in other words, was set not by physical conditions but by competition from a stronger neighbor.

Competition rarely just continues forever unresolved. Because it lowers survival, growth, or reproduction for the organisms involved, natural selection favors any trait that lets a competitor avoid or reduce the conflict. Over time this can push species toward using resources in different ways, or it can drive weaker competitors to decline or disappear from a shared area altogether. The next two chapters look closely at these outcomes: what happens, in strict theory, when two species compete for the exact same resource, and how species so often manage to keep sharing a landscape without one wiping out the other.
